passages.t: ‘How lovely is Your dwelling place’: the pilgrim's longing
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of the sons of Korah” (verse 1). It is a song of longing. “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts” (verse 1). “My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God” (verse 2).

The singer even envies the birds. “Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she places her young near Your altars” (verse 3). The small birds live where he longs to be.

Then he blesses two kinds of people. First, those who live in God's house and praise him all day (verse 4). Second, those on the road to get there. “Blessed are those whose strength is in You, whose hearts are set on pilgrimage” (verse 5). “As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs” (verse 6). “They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The sons of Korah were a family of temple singers. Their name heads several psalms that love the temple, as Psalms 42 and 43 did. Gittith, as the note on Psalm 81 says, is a word no one fully understands.

Israel's men were told to go up to God's house three times a year: “at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles” (Deuteronomy 16:16). For most families that meant days of walking on dusty roads, often with others from the same village. The word for ‘pilgrimage’ in verse 5 is close to a Hebrew word for a raised road or highway. The pilgrim's heart is on the road before the feet are.

No one knows where the Valley of Baca was. The name may be a kind of tree that grows in dry ground. The old Greek translation took it as ‘weeping’, so it became ‘the valley of weeping’. Either way, a dry, hard place becomes springs as God's people pass through it.

Birds nesting in the temple's walls and courts would have been a common sight.
passages.later:
Jesus told a woman at a well that a time was coming when people would worship the Father “neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John 4:21), but “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23).

Hebrews tells Christians, “you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). And Revelation ends with no temple at all, “because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21:22).
passages.asks:
What do you long for most? Psalm 84 is honest about an ache for God that the body itself feels. If you have that ache, it is not a fault. It is a sign that you were made for him.

And notice verse 6. The road to God may run through a valley of tears. The psalm does not say the valley is skipped. It says that those whose strength is in God find springs there.

passages.t: ‘Better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere’
passages.happening:
The singer prays. “O LORD God of Hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob” (verse 8). He prays for the king too: “look with favor on the face of Your anointed” (verse 9).

Then come the best-known lines. “For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked” (verse 10).

He says why. “For the LORD God is a sun and a shield; the LORD gives grace and glory; He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity” (verse 11).

The psalm ends with its third blessing. “O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
‘Your anointed’ (verse 9) is the king, and ‘our shield’ may be the king too. People prayed for their king at the temple. The note on Psalm 72 says more about prayers for the king.

A doorkeeper had the lowest job in the temple, standing at the threshold. The sons of Korah, by the account in Chronicles, were among those who guarded its thresholds (1 Chronicles 9:19). So a doorkeeper's job may have been the singer's own. He says he would rather have the humblest job in God's house than a fine life among the wicked.

‘Sun and shield’ is a rare pair. The sun gives light and life; the shield gives protection. God is both.

Look at the three blessings: those who live in God's house (verse 4), those on the road (verse 5), and those who trust him (verse 12). The last one is open to anyone, anywhere.
passages.later: Jesus said that he is the gate of the sheepfold (John 10:9). Paul wrote, “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32), much as verse 11 promises.
passages.hard: ‘He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity’ (verse 11). Does this mean that faithful people never lack anything? No. The Psalms themselves are full of faithful people who suffer, and Psalm 73 shows one wrestling with exactly this. The line speaks of God's goodness, and of what is truly good, as God sees it. It is not a promise of everything a person wants.
passages.asks:
Would you rather have one day near God than a thousand without him? Most of us would say yes, but our calendars may tell another story. Take one small step toward God's presence this week: time in worship, in prayer, or with his people.

And if the work you do for God feels small, remember the doorkeeper. Small work in God's house is still work in God's house.
